title: Invite-accept race causing role shadowing and intermittent permission errors during SSO/SAML provisioning
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Several customers have reported two related failure modes when joining organizations via email invite during SSO (SAML) sign-in: 1) Immediate permission denial to admin routes after accepting an invite, requiring re-login or support intervention; 2) In a few cases, transient over-permissioning for a single request (role shadowing) followed by automatic rollback. Both behaviors are intermittent and correlate with invite-accept flows and our SAML group sync path. This ticket tracks investigation, root cause, and a targeted bugfix for RBAC v2 user provisioning + audit logging coverage.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Create org invite for external user via console (invite token sent to email).
2) User clicks invite and attempts SSO sign-in (SAML IdP) on the same browser session, which triggers IdP assertion with group claims.

3) On first sign-in, backend hits /provision-user which: creates user record, applies invite role bindings, then triggers async SAML claim sync path that writes additional group->role mappings into RBAC store.
4) Observe either: A) immediate 403 on /api/admin/* endpoints (permission denied) OR B) one request returns 200 with elevated admin scope then subsequent requests drop to normal role set.
5) Repeating sign-in or forcing RBAC cache invalidation resolves the issue in most cases.
observed_behavior: Intermittent 403s immediately after invite acceptance; rare single-request elevation. Audit logs sometimes record actions under the pre-provisioned invite identity or show mismatched claim_source entries (missing SAML tag). Some affected customers opened escalations (#SUP-492, #SUP-517).
expected_behavior: Deterministic effective role calculation after invite acceptance and SAML claim processing: either final role set should be applied atomically before allowing protected requests or requests should be re-evaluated after claim sync. Audit logs should attribute events with correct claim_source and show role transition events.
root_cause: Race condition between synchronous invite-accept provisioning and asynchronous SAML group/claim sync. The provisioning path writes a baseline role set (invite binding) and returns an auth token before the SAML sync finishes. RBAC v2 caches effective_roles in Redis with a TTL and we do not hold a write lock while the async SAML updater mutates role bindings. Additionally, audit events emitted during the provisioning path omit a reliable claim_source tag and sometimes reference the temporary pre-provisioned user id, causing misattribution. Token refresh and session propagation paths do not trigger immediate role recomputation, leaving a window where API requests use stale role info.
proposed_fixes: A) Make invite-accept + SAML claim application atomic: change flow so that invite acceptance blocks returning final auth token until SAML claims are applied or a deterministic merge/resolution happens. Implement with short distributed lock on user:{id}:provision and idempotent claim application.

B) Update RBAC service to compute effective_roles synchronously when provisioning is in progress, and push cache invalidation/event when claims change. Ensure role computation is fast (memoize per-request) and guarded by the provision lock to avoid double-apply races.

C) Emit explicit audit events for 'provision:start','provision:claims_applied','provision:complete' with claim_source=SAML|INVITE and include before/after role snapshots. Fix audit logger to always use final persisted user_id and org_id.

D) Patch token refresh path: when a token is minted after provisioning, attach a role_version header and reject requests without matching role_version for the first 5s, forcing client SDK to refresh on mismatch (opt-in behind feature flag).
E) Add integration test coverage (SAML assertion + invite token acceptance race) and fuzz tests for concurrent claim writes.
implementation_notes: - Introduce Redis-based lease with 5s timeout for provisioning; use existing lock utility (util/redis-lock).
- Add new DB column 'role_version' on user_roles (string sha) and include it in tokens and audit events.
- Keep a feature flag rbac_v2_provision_lock to roll out gradually.
- Work with infra to ensure Redis latency is <10ms in staging to avoid blocking user sign-in paths.
- Maintain idempotency: provisioning should be safe to replay if webhook retries occur.
rollout_plan: 1) Merge patch behind feature flag and deploy to staging (staging-2025.02).
2) Run integration tests and reproduce prior failure mode in staging with support test accounts.
3) Enable feature flag for 5% of prod orgs (canary) for 24 hours, monitor SLOs and support queues.
4) Expand to 50% for 48 hours if no regressions, then full rollout.
5) Remove legacy path and feature flag after two weeks of stable metrics and sign-off from security.
test_plan: - Unit tests for new lock acquisition/release and role_version lifecycle.
- Integration tests: concurrent invite-accept + SAML claim push reproducer with deterministic scheduler.
- End-to-end QA: simulate customer flows (Invite->SSO) with Safari/Chrome sessions and mobile flows.
- Fuzz test: random delays on async claim consumer to ensure no stale behavior.
monitoring_queries: - COUNT by hour of 'permission_denied' (403) for endpoints matching /api/admin/* since deploy - compare to baseline.
- Alert if proportion of users with role_version mismatch between token and RBAC store > 0.1% in 5m windows.
- Audit-log anomaly query: events without claim_source tag in the last 7 days (should be zero).
- Support queue: tickets referencing 'invite' + '403' (SUP label) rolling 24h.
communications: - Internal: notify support, security, and account management channels with expected timeline and mitigation steps.
- Customer-facing: template for affected orgs explaining root cause, action taken, and how to verify restored behavior; offer support-assisted remediation if customers are blocked.
- Release notes: include short summary and opt-in instructions for early adopters of the feature flag.
